claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain relative to commercially used pure tungsten at high temperature.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten at high temperature.
A fine, stable, multicomponent precipitate network forms in WTaTiVZr.
The precipitate network impedes dislocation motion.
The precipitate network impedes crack propagation.
The precipitate network permits more homogeneous plastic deformation.
High-temperature annealing produces a fully homogenized WTaTiVZr initial state.
Similar annealing of WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten will provide comparable grain structures.
The structural mediator includes both fine-scale stable multielement precipitates and solid-solution effects in the alloy matrix.
The multicomponent nature of WTaTiVZr promotes formation of a fine precipitate network.
Dislocation hindrance by the precipitates delays strain localization and thereby increases ductility.
Crack deflection by the precipitate network increases toughness.
Limited slip systems and grain-boundary embrittlement dominate the high-temperature deformation and fracture behavior of pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature testing, WTaTiVZr will undergo more plastic deformation before failure than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature testing, WTaTiVZr will have greater fracture toughness than pure tungsten.
TEM or related characterization will reveal precipitate-mediated dislocation pinning in tested WTaTiVZr.
Fracture-path characterization will reveal precipitate-mediated crack deflection in tested WTaTiVZr.
The proposed mechanism applies only below temperatures at which the precipitates coarsen or dissolve.
Extreme irradiation may alter the precipitate structure enough to invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Failure to observe either enhanced plastic strain and toughness or a substantial precipitate network mediating dislocation or crack behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
